title: Ezra 6:1–12
context: Ezra 6:1–12 records Darius’s search and decree. The archives are searched, and a scroll is found at Achmetha, commonly identified with Ecbatana in Media. It records Cyrus’s decree that the house be rebuilt as a place of sacrifice, with dimensions and building materials given, the costs paid from the royal treasury, and the temple vessels returned. Darius orders Tattenai and his companions to stay away from the work, to pay its expenses from the royal taxes beyond the River, and to supply animals, grain, salt, wine, and oil for sacrifices, so that the priests may pray for the life of the king and his sons. Anyone who alters the decree is to be punished, and Darius calls on God to overthrow any king or people who tries to destroy the house. A cubit was about 18 inches. Compare Cyrus’s decree in Ezra 1:2–4, which differs in form and detail; these notes name the difference without harmonizing it. Both traditions see God’s providence turning an official inquiry into full royal support for the work.

verses.text: Then Darius the king made a decree, and the house of the archives, where the treasures were laid up in Babylon, was searched.
verses.arminianNotes: Darius orders a search in the archives where the treasures were kept in Babylon. Arminians see the king acting responsibly on the officials’ request, which allows God’s earlier work through Cyrus to come to light.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence in the search. Both traditions read the verse as an example of how God works through ordinary government procedures to accomplish his purposes.

verses.text: A scroll was found at Achmetha, in the palace that is in the province of Media, and in it this was written for a record:
verses.arminianNotes: A scroll is found at Achmetha in the province of Media. Arminian readers note that the record was found in a different place than expected, and they see God’s care in preserving it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the discovery as God’s providence. Achmetha is commonly identified with Ecbatana, a Persian royal residence, and both traditions hold the details of the archives with appropriate caution.

verses.text: In the first year of Cyrus the king, Cyrus the king made a decree: Concerning God’s house at Jerusalem, let the house be built, the place where they offer sacrifices, and let its foundations be strongly laid, with its height sixty cubits and its width sixty cubits;
verses.arminianNotes: The scroll records Cyrus’s decree that the house be rebuilt as a place for sacrifices, with its foundations strongly laid, sixty cubits high and sixty wide. A cubit was about 18 inches. Arminians see the decree providing for the restoration of sacrificial worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the dimensions differ from Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:2), and that the text does not explain the figures. Both traditions read the verse as confirming the official basis for the rebuilding.

verses.text: with three courses of great stones and a course of new timber. Let the expenses be given out of the king’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The decree specifies three courses of great stones and one of new timber, with the costs paid from the king’s house. Arminian readers see remarkable royal generosity toward the worship of Israel’s God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God moving a pagan king to fund his house. Both traditions read the verse as an example of God’s provision for his people through unexpected sources.

verses.text: Also let the gold and silver vessels of God’s house, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple which is at Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, be restored and brought again to the temple which is at Jerusalem, everything to its place. You shall put them in God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The decree orders the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar took to be returned to the temple in Jerusalem, each to its place. Arminians see the restoration of what was taken in judgment as a sign of God’s mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and recall Ezra 1:7–11 and 5:14–15. Both traditions read the verse as showing God’s faithfulness in restoring the worship of his house.

verses.text: Now therefore, Tattenai, governor beyond the River, Shetharbozenai, and your companions the Apharsachites, who are beyond the River, you must stay far from there.
verses.arminianNotes: Darius tells Tattenai, Shetharbozenai, and their companions to stay far from there. Arminian readers see the officials’ inquiry turned into an order to stop interfering, which protects the builders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence reversing the threat. Both traditions read the verse as the turning point of the episode, where the inquiry ends in protection for God’s people.

verses.text: Leave the work of this house of God alone; let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews build this house of God in its place.
verses.arminianNotes: Darius orders them to leave the work alone and let the governor and elders of the Jews build the house in its place. Arminians see God’s people freed to complete the work he had called them to do.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s purpose being carried out through the king’s command. Both traditions note that the governor of the Jews is not named here, and they avoid supplying an identification the text does not make.

verses.text: Moreover I make a decree regarding what you shall do for these elders of the Jews for the building of this house of God: that of the king’s goods, even of the tribute beyond the River, expenses must be given with all diligence to these men, that they not be hindered.
verses.arminianNotes: Darius orders that the expenses be paid from the royal taxes beyond the River, so the builders are not hindered. Arminian readers see God turning the resources of the empire toward his house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign provision. Both traditions note that the taxes collected by the officials who questioned the work now pay for it, and they read the reversal as shared ground.

verses.text: That which they have need of, including young bulls, rams, and lambs, for burnt offerings to the God of heaven; also wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the word of the priests who are at Jerusalem, let it be given them day by day without fail,
verses.arminianNotes: Darius orders that young bulls, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine, and oil be given daily as the priests require. Arminians see generous provision for the regular worship of God, according to the priests’ direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God supplying the needs of his worship. Both traditions read the verse as showing that the king’s support extended to the daily sacrifices, not only to the building.

verses.text: that they may offer sacrifices of pleasant aroma to the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king and of his sons.
verses.arminianNotes: The purpose is that they offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. Arminian readers see the king’s self-interest at work, and they also see God’s people able to pray for those in authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and compare the call to seek the welfare of the city in Jeremiah 29:7 and to pray for rulers in 1 Timothy 2:1–2. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about prayer for those who govern.

verses.text: I have also made a decree that whoever alters this message, let a beam be pulled out from his house, and let him be lifted up and fastened on it; and let his house be made a dunghill for this.
verses.arminianNotes: Darius decrees that anyone who alters the message will be impaled on a beam from his house and his house made a dunghill. Arminians read the harsh penalty as typical of Persian royal decrees, recorded by the text without endorsing its severity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as a historical record of the king’s authority. Both traditions see the penalty as showing how seriously the decree protected the work, without drawing a moral lesson from its cruelty.

verses.text: May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow all kings and peoples who stretch out their hand to alter this, to destroy this house of God which is at Jerusalem. I Darius have made a decree. Let it be done with all diligence.
verses.arminianNotes: Darius prays that the God who caused his name to dwell there will overthrow any king or people who tries to destroy the house. Arminian readers see a pagan king acknowledging the God of Israel and his chosen place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s name honored even in a foreign decree. Both traditions note the echo of Deuteronomy’s language about the place where God causes his name to dwell (compare Deuteronomy 12:11), and they read the verse as shared ground.
